notes: Advertisement discontinuance appeal; Sullivan J's analysis of Regulation 8 and conservation area duty is detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Clear Channel v SoS: advertisement discontinuance and conservation area duty

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Control of Advertisements) Regulations 1992
Planning (Listed Buildings and Conservation Areas) Act 1990

key_facts: Clear Channel appealed against an inspector's dismissal of its appeal against a discontinuance notice for large illuminated poster panels at a Clerkenwell car park site.
The panels had deemed consent after express temporary consent in 1993 but had remained for over ten years adjacent to a Grade II listed public house in a conservation area.
The claimant argued the inspector wrongly treated longevity as decisive, failed to assess net visual amenity including screening, and misapplied the substantial injury test.
The council argued the inspector correctly exercised powers under Regulation 8 and could have regard to section 72 conservation area duties.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court section 288 challenge to an advertisement appeal inspector's decision.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the inspector lawfully found substantial injury to amenity and the section 72 duty applied to decisions under the Advertisement Regulations.
enrichment.ratio: Regulation 8 requires necessity to remedy substantial injury to amenity, not mere inappropriateness; an inspector may weigh prior temporary consent and screening arguments, and decisions under advertisement regulations are functions by virtue of the principal planning Act so section 72 conservation area duties apply.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector applied the correct Regulation 8 substantial injury test
Whether longevity of deemed-consent advertisements was a relevant or decisive factor
Whether net visual amenity including screening had to be assessed
Whether section 72(1) applied to advertisement discontinuance decisions

notes: Renewed sentence appeal; facts and Single Judge reasoning are straightforward.

enrichment.short_title: R v Rix: six-year concurrent sentence for burglary, fraud and blackmail
key_facts: Rix burgled a vulnerable schizophrenic neighbour's flat, stole property and documents, obtained a credit card using the victim's details, and blackmailed him with false paedophile threats.
The victim suffered severe anxiety, loss of stability and inability to continue his studies; the offences were premeditated and targeted.
Rix had a long earlier record but a twelve-year gap before these offences, following bereavement after his wife and son were killed.
He pleaded guilty at the earliest opportunity, showed remorse on sentence, and had addressed drug and alcohol misuse on remand.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for leave to appeal against sentence after refusal by the Single Judge.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; the six-year concurrent total, though stern, was not manifestly excessive.
enrichment.ratio: Blackmail targeting a highly vulnerable victim with devastating foreseeable psychological effects is particularly serious; mitigation including guilty pleas and remorse does not make a stern but not excessive total sentence manifestly wrong.
legal_issues: Whether six years' imprisonment was manifestly excessive for concurrent burglary, deception and blackmail
Weight of deliberate targeting and vulnerability of the victim
Mitigation from guilty pleas, remorse and prior gap in offending
linked_authorities: R v Davis [2004] 1 Cr App R(S) 31

notes: Complex inquest JR on causation, neglect and Middleton narrative verdicts; Mitting J's analysis is thorough.

enrichment.short_title: Longfield Care Homes: inquest neglect direction and narrative verdict

statutes_considered.title: Fatal Accidents and Sudden Deaths Inquiry (Scotland) Act 1976

key_facts: Mrs Hall, an elderly dementia resident, fell from an unattended open lounge window at Longfield Care Home and died about nineteen hours later from bronchopneumonia.
Pathology evidence indicated pneumonia predated the fall and would likely have caused death within a similar timeframe, though possibly one or two days later.
The jury returned accidental death to which neglect contributed after the coroner left neglect based largely on a missing written window risk assessment.
The care home sought judicial review of the verdict and the coroner's directions on causation and neglect.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a coroner's inquest verdict and summing-up.
enrichment.outcome: Verdict quashed and replaced with a narrative finding; Galbraith sufficiency to leave causation was upheld but the neglect direction materially misdirected on risk assessment as civil negligence.
enrichment.ratio: A coroner may leave accidental death where Galbraith is satisfied, but neglect is a term of art requiring gross failure to provide basic care with a clear causal link, not mere absence of a risk assessment; where death results from mixed causes a Middleton narrative verdict should be used.
legal_issues: Whether the coroner should have left accidental death and neglect verdicts
Whether there was sufficient evidence the fall contributed to the timing of death
Whether the neglect direction conflated negligence with gross neglect
Appropriate narrative verdict after R (Middleton) v West Somerset Coroner
linked_authorities: R v Inner London Coroner ex parte Douglas Williams [1999] 1 All ER 344
R (Middleton) v West Somerset Coroner [2004] 2 WLR 800
R v Her Majesty's Coroner for North Humberside ex parte Jamieson [1995] QB 1

notes: Single ground appeal on jury discussion warning; strong prosecution case noted.

enrichment.short_title: R v Edwards: handling appeal over omitted jury discussion warning

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: Edwards was convicted after trial of handling stolen Land Rover parts assembled from multiple stolen vehicles, including a cab and identification plates.
He claimed innocent purchase and respray but the prosecution relied on the volume of stolen parts and a allegedly forged receipt.
The trial judge did not expressly warn the jury not to discuss the case with outsiders, though jurors had likely seen an introductory video.
There was no evidence any juror had improper discussions during the short three-day trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by leave of the Single Judge on one procedural ground.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; omission of the standard warning did not render the conviction unsafe given no suggestion of improper discussion and very strong evidence.
enrichment.ratio: Failure to remind jurors not to discuss the case with non-jurors is an error, but the verdict is not necessarily unsafe where there is no evidence of breach and the prosecution case is extremely strong.
legal_issues: Whether the judge's omission to warn jurors against external discussion made the verdict unsafe
Application of R v Oliver and R v Burley
Effect of jury induction video and absence of evidence of impropriety
linked_authorities: R v Oliver [1996] 2 Cr App R(S) 514

notes: Twin human rights appeals on heterosexual-only partner definitions in child support and housing benefit; long judgment.

enrichment.short_title: SSWP v M and Langley: same-sex partner definitions and Article 14

statutes_considered.title: Child Support (Maintenance Assessments and Special Cases) Regulations 1992
Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992

key_facts: M, a non-resident parent in a same-sex relationship, successfully argued before the Commissioner that child support regulations treating opposite-sex partners differently breached her Convention rights.
Ms Langley was denied housing benefit because she paid rent to a former opposite-sex partner under an anti-abuse provision that would not apply to a former same-sex partner.
Both schemes define partner and unmarried couple as a man and a woman living together as husband and wife.
The Secretary of State appealed M's success; Ms Langley appealed her failure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated Court of Appeal appeals from Social Security Commissioner decisions.
enrichment.outcome: Secretary of State's appeal allowed in M's case; Ms Langley's appeal dismissed because Article 8 was not sufficiently engaged.
enrichment.ratio: Article 14 requires the circumstances to fall within the ambit of another Convention right; child support liability adjustments and withholding housing benefit under anti-abuse rules do not sufficiently engage Article 8 or Article 1 Protocol 1 merely because they affect finances or housing choices.
legal_issues: Whether child support partner pooling rules discriminate unlawfully against same-sex couples
Whether Regulation 7 housing benefit anti-abuse rules engage Article 8
Ambit of Article 14 with Articles 8 and Protocol 1 Article 1
Justification and comparator analysis for heterosexual-only definitions
linked_authorities: Douglas v Secretary of State for Work and Pensions [2004] EWCA Civ 1407

notes: Urgent trade union ballot notice appeal; special group facts emphasised.

enrichment.short_title: EWS v RMT: trade union ballot notices to group companies

statutes_considered.title: Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992

key_facts: RMT balloted engineering and groundstaff for industrial action during a dispute headed 'Breakdown in Industrial Relations - EWS'.
Notices under sections 226A and 234A were sent only to EWS Ltd's corporate industrial relations manager though EWSI Ltd employees were listed on attached schedules.
EWS and EWSI operated joint industrial relations through one manager under a partnership agreement treating both as 'the company'.
Wilkie J continued injunctions because RMT did not objectively give notice to EWSI Ltd.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Urgent appeal against continuation of injunctions restraining industrial action.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the section 226A ballot notice was valid notice to both EWS and EWSI on the special facts.
enrichment.ratio: Section 226A and 234A notices must be construed objectively in context; where two group companies negotiate jointly through one industrial relations manager and schedules identify both companies' sites, a notice addressed to 'the company' can reasonably be notice to both employers despite separate corporate identity.
legal_issues: Whether RMT gave valid section 226A notice to EWSI Ltd
Relevance of union official's subjective intention not to notify EWSI
Objective construction of notices in a joint industrial relations context
Strict compliance with trade union notice requirements

notes: Important equal pay reference on Danfoss and justification; EAT errors identified.

enrichment.short_title: Cadman v HSE: equal pay, length of service and Danfoss reference
key_facts: Mrs Cadman, an HSE band 2 inspector, claimed equal pay with four male comparators paid more mainly because of longer incremental service.
The employment tribunal upheld her indirect sex discrimination claim and ordered a declaration modifying her pay term.
The EAT allowed HSE's appeal, holding Danfoss meant length of service needed no specific justification and the tribunal misapplied Bilka.
Evidence showed women in the relevant workforce had shorter average service than men.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Employee appeal to the Court of Appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal.
enrichment.outcome: Reference to the ECJ ordered on Danfoss; if resolved in Cadman's favour the justification issue would be remitted to a fresh tribunal.
enrichment.ratio: Later ECJ cases cast doubt on Danfoss's blanket dispensation for length-of-service pay differentials; the employment tribunal's justification analysis contained legal errors including treating after-the-event justification as impermissible and requiring strict necessity rather than reasonable necessity.
legal_issues: Whether Danfoss still exempts length of service from objective justification
Whether after-the-event justification is permissible under Bilka
Correct application of the reasonable necessity test
Individual versus collective justification in equal pay claims
linked_authorities: Handels-og Kontorfunktionaerenes Forbund I Danmark v Dansk Arbejdsgiverforening (Danfoss) [1989] ECR 3199
Bilka-Kaufhaus GmbH v Weber von Hartz [1987] ICR 110
Barry v Midland Bank plc [1999] ICR 319

confidence.notes: Danfoss outcome depends on ECJ reference but domestic justification errors are clearly identified.

notes: Urgent interim injunction with arbitration stay argument; document ownership analysis is clear.

enrichment.short_title: NIG v Young: interim return of policy documents despite arbitration clause
key_facts: NIG, an insurer, terminated a delegation agreement under which Young issued after-the-event litigation insurance policies on its behalf.
NIG sought an interim injunction requiring return of policy databases and documents needed to manage unresolved claims.
Young remained willing to manage claims but NIG alleged material breaches including failure to keep NIG informed.
Young invoked a clause 10 arbitration agreement and argued the court should adjourn pending a section 9 stay.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application for interim mandatory injunction in urgent committal-related commercial dispute.
enrichment.outcome: Interim injunction granted for document return and related relief; urgency justified immediate relief under section 44(3) despite the arbitration clause.
enrichment.ratio: A tort or agency claim for conversion or delivery up of documents evidencing policies belongs to the principal insurer and is not necessarily barred by an arbitration clause; where urgency and policyholder distress require immediate preservation of evidence, section 44(3) permits interim orders before arbitration.
legal_issues: Whether the claim was confined to contractual disputes caught by the arbitration clause
Ownership of policy records held by a terminated coverholder agent
Whether the court should adjourn pending section 9 stay
Availability of section 44(3) urgent interim relief

notes: Fresh evidence application refused; procedural fairness concerns noted regarding appeal grounds.

enrichment.short_title: Sun Bank v Wootten: Ladd v Marshall refusal on mortgage signature evidence
key_facts: Sun Bank sought possession of the Woottens' home based on a legal charge Mrs Wootten claimed was forged.
The recorder preferred witness evidence that she had signed the mortgage and dismissed the defence.
After trial Mrs Wootten sought to adduce fresh evidence from Mrs Dursley allegedly admitting forgery of a deed of consent and related documents.
Mrs Dursley withdrew the mortgage-deed admission before appeal, would not testify, and her recorded statements contradicted her trial evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal seeking permission to rely on fresh evidence and a retrial in possession proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused and appeal dismissed; no retrial ordered under Ladd v Marshall or CPR discretion.
enrichment.ratio: Fresh evidence must be unavailable with reasonable diligence, credible, and likely to affect the result; inconsistent second-hand statements from a witness who will not give evidence and who lied at trial cannot satisfy Ladd v Marshall or justify a retrial.
legal_issues: Application of Ladd v Marshall criteria after the CPR
Whether taped conversations with Mrs Dursley constituted new evidence
Whether a retrial was workable if the witness refused to testify
Standard of proof for forgery allegations in possession claims
linked_authorities: Hertfordshire Investments Ltd v Bubb [2000] 1 WLR 2318

notes: Major CLS costs set-off appeal; lengthy review of Lockley and legal aid jurisprudence.

enrichment.short_title: Burkett v Hammersmith: CLS costs set-off after successful delay appeal
key_facts: Mrs Burkett, CLS-funded, challenged Imperial Wharf planning permission over environmental assessment inadequacies.
She won on time limits in the House of Lords but lost on the merits before Newman J.
Newman J ordered the council's substantive success costs to be set off against costs the council owed her from the House of Lords delay appeal.
The appeal concerned whether a CLS-funded claimant's costs belong to the LSC so as to prevent mutuality of set-off.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against costs order following unsuccessful substantive judicial review.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Lockley applies and Newman J lawfully ordered costs set-off in the same proceedings.
enrichment.ratio: A costs set-off ordered under section 51 is an exercise of judicial discretion, not equitable mutuality; costs orders remain those of the assisted party and may be set off against other costs in the same action despite CLS funding regulations.
legal_issues: Whether Lockley permits set-off of CLS-funded costs against adverse costs
Whether the LSC is the true beneficiary preventing mutuality
Costs protection under section 11 Access to Justice Act 1999
Discretionary nature of costs set-off versus Hanak v Green rules
linked_authorities: Lockley v National Blood Transfusion Service [1992] 1 WLR 492
